title: Leveraged carry trade portfolios
abstract: Studying all possible pairs of 11 major currencies and 11 portfolios in 1976-2008 we show that, when there is no leverage, carry trade is significantly profitable for most currency pairs and portfolios. Positive returns do not diminish in time providing a strong case against the hypothesis of uncovered interest rate parity. We explain these findings with the leveraged nature of carry trade: leverage may increase profitability but it materially increases downside risk. We argue that market inefficiency is related to the level of leverage.
summary_en: The 'carry trade' (borrow in low-yield currencies, invest in high-yield ones) is a famous market anomaly that violates the uncovered interest-rate parity hypothesis. Darvas studies all 110 currency-pair combinations among 11 major currencies and 11 portfolios over 1976-2008. Without leverage, carry trade is significantly profitable for most pairs and shows no diminishing returns over time — hard evidence against UIP. With leverage, profitability rises but downside risk increases far more than proportionally. The market inefficiency is fundamentally tied to the leverage level used by speculators.
data_used: Daily exchange-rate and short-term interest-rate data for 11 major currencies (USD, EUR, JPY, GBP, CHF, AUD, CAD, NZD, SEK, NOK, ZAR-equivalent) over 1976-2008, with all bilateral pairs and 11 currency-portfolio strategies tested.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for MNB foreign-exchange supervision and macroprudential limits on Hungarian banks' FX exposure. The paper documents that carry-trade returns are systematic and persistent — relevant for MNB stress testing of bank FX-funding positions and for Pénzügyminisztérium analysis of HUF carry-trade dynamics.
